candidateRows: A viable ethical framework must avoid both religious fundamentalism and moral relativism while reducing unnecessary suffering.
This establishes Peterson's initial account of the shared ethical problem and identifies the two opposing failures that the debate must navigate.
Peterson begins by reconstructing Harris's position, identifying fundamentalism, relativism, and unnecessary suffering as the central ethical concerns.
Well-being encompasses both the mitigation of suffering and every positive possibility available to conscious beings.
The move defines Harris's foundational moral criterion and connects his secular framework to both suffering and positive conscious experience.
Peterson's suffering-centered reconstruction of Harris's ethical foundation.
Harris accepts the concern with suffering but broadens the moral foundation to an elastic conception of well-being covering all positive forms of being.
Moral realism holds that questions of human value have discoverable right and wrong answers independent of what perpetrators happen to want.
This is the core secular moral-realist thesis, rejecting relativism and presenting moral progress as discovery about value, suffering, and flourishing.
Peterson's suggestion that agreement may be easiest by concentrating first on outcomes people do not want.
Harris closes the door on relativism by arguing that even people who desire atrocity can be wrong and that humanity must discover better answers about value.
The danger of arbitrary absolutism is grounded in human tendencies toward fundamentalism generally, not uniquely in religious belief.
The distinction challenges the secular critique's causal focus by arguing that dogmatic absolutism also appears in nonreligious totalitarian systems.
Harris's framing of religious fundamentalism as a principal source of arbitrary moral injunction.
Peterson accepts moral realism and human universals but contends that the relevant pathology is fundamentalism across religious and secular systems alike.
Religion deserves special scrutiny because it uniquely treats dogma and belief without compelling evidence as virtues rather than defects.
This supplies the differentiating premise needed for Harris's focus on religion despite acknowledging that dogmatism can also occur in secular settings.
Peterson's claim that fundamentalism is a general pathology rather than one specifically associated with religion.
Harris concedes broader dogmatism but argues that religion is distinctive in positively valuing faith and dogma despite the absence of compelling evidence.
Twentieth-century totalitarian atrocities were not products of atheism; their operative evil was religion-like dogmatism that prevented correction through inquiry.
The response contests a major counterexample to secularism and relocates the cause of totalitarian violence in enforced, unrevisable dogma rather than atheism.
Peterson's challenge that Nazi and Soviet dogmas were as pernicious as religious dogmas and may implicate atheism.
Harris argues that fascist movements were not straightforwardly atheist and that Stalinism and North Korea reproduce religious structures of cult, apostasy, and coercion.
Authentic spiritual experience may be real, but its truths must be expressed through universal facts about consciousness rather than culturally contingent dogmas.
The move preserves spirituality within a secular framework while denying that historical accidents or inherited doctrines can establish universal spiritual truth.
The moderator's suggestion that removing dogmatism may leave a defensible nondogmatic religious remainder.
Harris accepts religious art and genuine changes in consciousness but argues that spiritual truth must transcend founders, cultures, languages, and historical contingencies.
Chimpanzee coalitionary violence shows that tribal atrocity has evolutionary roots deeper than religious doctrine or secular ideology.
The evolutionary counterexample challenges explanations that assign primary causal responsibility for group atrocity to surface-level religious or ideological propositions.
Harris's account of dogmatic belief as the central mechanism behind religious and totalitarian violence.
Peterson recounts chimpanzee border raids and argues that comparable atrocity without religion or totalitarian ideology reveals a more fundamental tribal substrate.
Although tribal aggression is not unique to religion, sincere religious doctrines can independently lead otherwise decent people toward extreme and unnecessary suffering.
This answers the evolutionary objection by distinguishing background tribal impulses from harms rationally produced by wholehearted acceptance of religious propositions.
Peterson's argument that chimpanzee aggression makes the roots of atrocity deeper than religious belief or ideology.
Harris acknowledges nonreligious tribal violence but cites conversion, salvation, hell, sexuality, and scriptural finality as ideas capable of generating avoidable harms themselves.
Many scriptural commands are unambiguous, ethically inferior, and resistant to revision, so making religion palatable keeps modern societies tied to Iron Age morality.
The move presents Harris's strongest text-based case that inherited religious authority obstructs moral progress even when interpreters are sincere and psychologically ordinary.
Peterson's claim that fundamentalists conflate an allegedly perfect text with their fallible interpretation of that text.
Harris argues that commands concerning punishment and slavery require little interpretation, can motivate ordinary believers, and impede a fully modern conversation about ethics.
Individual biblical sentences must be interpreted within the developmental structure of the entire narrative, whose later portions condition the meaning of its earlier portions.
This supplies Peterson's principal method for resisting isolated literal readings of morally objectionable passages and grounds his broader defense of biblical interpretation.
The prior challenge that some religious passages are plainly wrong without any interpretive complication.

After Harris asks whether modern readers can identify unambiguously unacceptable scriptural claims, Peterson distinguishes religious traditions and argues that a complex canonical narrative must be interpreted as an integrated whole.
Narrative context and the New Testament do not rehabilitate explicit biblical rules governing conquest, killing, enslavement, and obedience by slaves.
The objection tests Peterson's interpretive defense against concrete prescriptive passages whose moral content appears stable even when placed within the full canon.
Peterson's claim that earlier biblical material must be read in light of the narrative's later development.
Harris moves from the abstract issue of narrative coherence to laws of war, arguing that explicit instructions remain brutal and unacceptable even under a canonical reading.
Treating scripture as divine revelation traps believers into defending an historically assembled canon containing plainly immoral commands that ordinary moral judgment can reject directly.
This directly supports the secular case that revelation and canonical authority obstruct moral correction rather than reliably grounding moral truth.
Peterson's effort to preserve psychological truths within scripture through contextual and developmental interpretation.

After agreement that religious traditions may contain psychological insights, Harris distinguishes selective recovery of insight from revelation, which obliges believers to retain the canon's morally repugnant passages.
Revelation can be read psychologically as depicting the recurring collapse of human orders and the redemptive emergence of heroic truthful speech under catastrophic conditions.
The move demonstrates Peterson's positive interpretive method and argues that biblical symbolism preserves actionable psychological truth despite troubling literal imagery.
Harris's argument that apocalyptic prophecy is dangerous, frightening, and historically conducive to destructive expectations.

Responding to Harris's critique of eschatology, Peterson brackets metaphysical certainty and interprets apocalypse as a pattern of personal and social dissolution in which truthful speech enables redemption.

Nonliteral theology becomes progressively less constrained by scripture, allowing interpreters to project modern moral and psychological insights onto texts whose literal meanings are barbaric or false.
This challenges the epistemic legitimacy of religious reinterpretation and supports replacing scriptural authority with open, independently constrained inquiry.
Peterson's claim that biblical symbolism can validly disclose psychological truths such as redemption through truthful speech.

Harris concedes that interpretations vary in plausibility but argues that increasingly metaphorical readings lose textual constraint, while literal readings preserve dangerous apocalyptic and exclusivist commitments.
Christianity embodies the shared antidote to dogmatism and totalitarianism—free truthful expression—not merely as an abstract proposition but as the incarnated redemptive personality of the Word.
This is a direct constructive defense of Christian symbolism as a uniquely embodied vehicle for a moral principle both debaters regard as indispensable.
Harris's contention that metaphorical interpretation is unconstrained and cannot vindicate the authority of Christian scripture.

Peterson begins from shared opposition to pathological dogmatism and argues that Christianity personifies truthful speech as the redemptive Word, making the tradition's symbolic form morally significant.
Facts cannot yield values without an antecedent interpretive framework, and that framework may be best understood partly as a personality or story rather than as bare propositions.
This states Peterson's fundamental objection to secular fact-based moral realism and identifies narrative structure as a necessary mediator between reality and value.
Harris's project of grounding moral values in objectively true facts without relying on religious narrative.

Peterson acknowledges the desire for objective moral grounding but argues that observation is never framework-free, then asks Harris to explain the prior structure through which facts acquire normative significance.
The intuition of objective reality is more fundamental than religion and remains the indispensable basis for knowledge, communication, prediction, and distinguishing perception from fantasy.
The move supplies a secular foundation for truth and inquiry that does not depend on stories, directly countering the claimed priority of narrative interpretive frameworks.
Peterson's proposal that access to facts requires an a priori framework best understood partly as story or personality.

Harris accepts that inquiry ultimately rests on unanalyzed intuitions but argues that reality-directed cognition is deeper than mythology and anchors both personal sanity and intersubjective reasoning.

Harris's own moral framework escapes infinite regress by contrasting narrative images of extreme suffering and flourishing, effectively relying on story-like moral intuitions analogous to hell and heaven.
This argues that secular moral realism covertly depends on the same narrative abstractions and foundational moral images that religious language makes explicit.
Harris's claim that foundational intuitions can ground objective inquiry without being best represented by religious stories.

Peterson compares mathematical intuitions with narrative moral intuitions, then interprets Harris's contrast between maximal misery and a good life as an abstraction toward the religious poles of hell and heaven.
The worst possible misery for every conscious being is intrinsically bad, and this foundational intuition makes all other uses of moral terms intelligible without requiring God or religious doctrine.
This is the core secular moral-realist grounding claim: universal suffering provides a nonreligious terminus for normative reasoning and the meaning of better and worse.
Peterson's objection that Harris merely stakes an a priori moral proposition rather than establishing an objectively factual truth.

Harris defines maximal universal misery across humans, animals, artificial minds, and unknown beings, then argues that denying its badness would empty all ordinary value judgments of coherent meaning.
Moral facts require interpretive intuitions, often embodied in stories, that distinguish suffering from the malevolent agency producing it.
The move directly challenges a purely suffering-centered moral landscape by arguing that narrative intuitions and malevolent intention are indispensable moral categories.
Harris's claim that universal suffering supplies a sufficient factual foundation for moral judgment.
After accepting the practical role of Harris's limiting case, Peterson argues that facts require intermediary intuitions and that hell also concerns the malevolent actions responsible for suffering.
A consequentialist account of well-being can include intentions, character, relationships, and every psychological consequence without reducing morality to bodily harm.
This response protects Harris's central framework from the objection that it excludes malevolence, character, intention, or the internal consequences of wrongdoing.
Peterson's objection that Harris's account treats suffering as distinct from the malevolent pleasure and intention producing it.
Harris clarifies that his moral landscape includes the mental states, intentions, character defects, social relations, and downstream consequences associated with harmful conduct.
Religious heuristics merit less concern when they improve well-being, but literal fundamentalism gains persuasive force precisely from plainly stated textual atrocities.
The move concedes possible religious utility while explaining why textual clarity gives fundamentalists an argumentative advantage and makes reformist reinterpretation unstable.
The proposed possibility that religious texts function as beneficial evolutionary heuristics that reliably increase well-being.

Harris conditionally accepts useful religious heuristics, then argues that fundamentalists can appeal directly to unambiguous commands while moderates import external values to sanitize inherited dogma.
Religious tradition can subordinate inherited dogma to the higher value of truthful inquiry, allowing knowledge to be updated rather than frozen in the past.
This is a direct religious-pragmatist answer to the charge that evolved traditions are obsolete, presenting open truth-seeking as internal to profound religious symbolism.
The argument that evolved religious stories reflect past environments and therefore cannot be trusted as timeless guides.
Peterson agrees that traditions require revision but contends that their deepest layer places the process of truthful knowledge updating above reliance on fixed dogma.
God can be understood as the transpersonal reality expressed through truthful speech, evolved valuation, conscience, sacrifice, judgment, and long-term social selection.
The move supplies Peterson's principal affirmative account of God-language and connects it to truth, evolution, moral hierarchy, conscience, sacrifice, and human flourishing.
Harris's request for a precise account of the God whose existence Peterson says he acts as though he accepts.
Peterson presents God as a collective representation of consciousness across time and as the highest value manifested through truth, conscience, sacrifice, competence, and selection.
Peterson's abstract definition of God omits the personal supernatural agent ordinarily meant by believers and changes the traditional noun rather than defending it.
This objection attacks whether Peterson's pragmatic God-language addresses the religious proposition at issue or merely redescribes secular psychological and social realities.
Peterson's definition of God as evolved truth, conscience, hierarchy, sacrifice, and long-term transpersonal reality.

Harris argues that Peterson's account lacks the prayer-answering personal deity commonly professed by believers and analogizes the redefinition to relabeling ordinary relations with the unseen as ghosts.
Penitent self-examination can function as answered prayer by eliciting an unwelcome but corrective insight into wrongdoing and possible restitution.
The example gives concrete pragmatic content to answered prayer without requiring an immediately specified supernatural mechanism, linking God-language to moral transformation.
Peterson asks the wrongdoer to confess sincerely, seek knowledge of the fault and its remedy, and accept whatever answer appears, predicting that such prayer produces a difficult response.
The described experience of answered prayer is familiar human psychology and does not require either supernatural causation or divine authorship of scripture.
The reply grants the psychological phenomenon while denying that it supports religious metaphysics, preserving the secular explanation of moral self-correction.
Peterson's claim that sincere penitential inquiry is a prayer that will reliably receive a corrective answer.
Harris recognizes the introspective process but argues that ordinary psychology explains it and that it supplies no basis for supernatural mechanisms or scriptural revelation.
Incompatible religious traditions assign conflicting meanings to good and evil, so their usefulness points toward a deeper reality rather than the truth of any one tradition.
The move challenges the epistemic authority of biblical tradition by showing that similarly meaningful religious systems yield irreconcilable moral interpretations.
The suggestion that evolved religious stories preserve useful patterns whose authors need not have consciously understood their significance.
Harris observes that Hindu and Buddhist stories can reverse Christian moral valences while remaining useful to adherents, implying that no single tradition explains their common utility.
Religious pluralism threatens nihilism unless inquiry identifies cross-domain patterns whose recurrence constrains interpretation and indicates an underlying reality.
The response acknowledges conflicting traditions while offering a fact-sensitive method for finding deeper recurrent structures and limiting arbitrary interpretation.
Harris's argument that useful but irreconcilable Christian, Hindu, and Buddhist systems require a deeper nonsectarian explanation.

Peterson says awareness of equally useful incompatible systems can destroy belief itself, then proposes seeking patterns repeated across religion, biology, philosophy, neuroscience, emotion, and play.
Religious and cultural variation undermines the claim that supposedly universal moral patterns recur consistently across traditions.
The objection tests whether religious narratives can supply universal moral structure despite sharply divergent cultural assumptions.
Peterson's claim that recurring patterns across domains reduce the likelihood of merely delusional interpretation.

After Peterson invokes convergence among multiple disciplines and traditions, Harris argues that cultures can invert allegedly shared moral concepts and that common humanity lies beneath religious overlays.
Cultural moral differences can coexist with deeper universals, just as diverse languages and stories share structures that identify their common form.
This supplies a central defense of extracting canonical moral structure from diverse stories without denying surface-level variation.
Harris's objection that cultures and religions vary too greatly to support universal moral patterns.
Peterson concedes local adaptations but argues that stories exhibit cross-context commonality and that even factual judgment depends upon prior intuitions that inquiry cannot wholly escape.
Moral intuitions form a hierarchy in which the deepest principles remain valid across contexts and orient judgments of better and worse lives.
The hierarchy explains how Peterson distinguishes profound moral universals from parochial impulses while preserving an objective moral orientation.
Harris's warning that reliance on intuition does not make every claimed intuition equally credible.
Following agreement that some intuitions are unreliable, Peterson compares moral principles with scientific truths whose depth is measured by their applicability across time and context.
Calling a deep moral orientation God is misleading because ordinary audiences usually understand that word in a substantially different religious sense.
The argument directly challenges whether pragmatic reinterpretation can responsibly retain conventional religious language without reinforcing dogmatic beliefs.
Peterson's identification of the deepest context-independent moral orientation with what may be called God.
Harris grants that Peterson's abstract moral principle is unobjectionable but distinguishes it from the meaning most believers attach to divinity and worries that the shared label obscures that gap.
Ambiguous religious language has harmful communicative effects because it permits conventional believers to hear validation that the speaker may not actually endorse.
This moves beyond semantic disagreement to a consequential critique of religious pragmatism as public communication that can shelter literal dogma.
Peterson's defense that he has not claimed his account of divinity is identical to what other religious people mean.

Harris compares Peterson's communication problem to rhetoric that preserves audience misconceptions, then contrasts Peterson's position with literalist beliefs about scripture, resurrection, judgment, and hell.
Religious heuristics are unreliable because they can produce adaptive behavior for mistaken reasons and cannot adjust reliably when circumstances change.
The claim states the secular alternative's core advantage: revisable reasoning can preserve valid concerns without depending on fixed mythic explanations.
The proposed reconciliation that religious stories may be retained as fitness-enhancing behavioral heuristics.

After a synthesis presents sexual prohibitions as potentially adaptive stories, Harris argues that useful fictions become obsolete while reality-based explanations can address pornography and social harms directly.
Rational educational interventions often have little power to change fundamental behavior, so purely reasoned explanation may be behaviorally insufficient.
The behavioral-efficacy objection supports the pragmatic case for culturally embodied narratives rather than relying exclusively on explicit rational instruction.
Harris's claim that pornography and sexual conduct can be addressed through rational psychological and sociological discussion.
Peterson answers the secular explanatory proposal by arguing that education about sex, condoms, and other basic behaviors often yields much less behavioral change than rationalists expect.
Dogmatic religious systems remain vulnerable to every new discovery because inherited rules track outcomes blindly rather than identifying the variables that actually matter.
This is a central epistemic argument for secular inquiry over fixed tradition: causal understanding supersedes accidentally useful inherited taboos.
Peterson's contention that rational education is no more behaviorally effective than inherited religious constraints.
Harris grants that traditions may once have encoded survival-enhancing practices but argues that discovery of the real causal mechanisms dissolves arbitrary prohibitions and improves guidance.
A worldview continuously corrected by honest engagement with reality is preferable to one anchored in unchanging ideas formed without modern investigative tools.
The proposition directly articulates the secular side of the debate's governing contrast between open inquiry and inherited dogmatic authority.
Peterson's warning that Enlightenment-centered accounts understate the long historical development behind modern rationality.
Harris acknowledges that enlightenment remains incomplete but presses for agreement that revisable contact with evidence offers better guidance than doctrines fixed by ancient limitations.
Evolution has produced implicit interpretive structures that mediate human access to facts and ground moral intuition but cannot be derived from present facts alone.
This closing argument supplies the deepest theoretical basis for Peterson's claim that moral value requires inherited interpretive structure beyond bare empirical facts.
Harris's claim that continuous engagement with presently apprehensible reality should replace anchoring in inherited ideas.

Peterson accepts that some obsolete principles should change but argues that profound intuitions reflect evolutionary structures formed through life's long interaction with reality and shared by both moral frameworks.
